Save this light alone, the room was nearly impossibly dark. My captors, seated on stools before me, cast long shadows onto the walls behind them from my bright shackles. Their faces were impossible to pick out. 
 
 ** “ We have studied your race for nearly a millennium. You are a simple race, yet there is one power you possess that even our high prophets fail to comprehend. ” ** 
 
 I felt beads of sweat fall down the sides of my face, salty as they breached the corners of my mouth. I looked at my still wife, her chest rising and falling. 
 
 ** “ Explain to us your power of sight. ” ** 
 
 My power of sight? To be honest my sight was failing me. I can no longer read the paper without putting on glasses. Frankly, I never thought of vision as a power, much less something that a far superior alien race would not understand. 
 
 ** “ Speak, human, if you wish to live. ” ** 
 
 “ Sight, ” I began. I looked up, trying to use the luminous bindings around my wrist to see the dark figures before me. “ Sight is the gateway into understanding the world. Sight gives meaning to every other sense of the body. When I am moving somewhere, I always am confident in my motions. When I am still, I can understand everything that is around me. ” 
 I paused for a moment, with a short grunt of curiosity demanding more, “ F-F-Food tastes better when I can see what I am about to eat. The most delicious looking fruit is the juiciest. A-and the brightest birds sing the loveliest songs. Whenever I hear something, I can use my vision to identify the source of the sound... ” I paused again and stole a look at my still unconscious wife laying on the ground, her brown hair a mess behind her, “ and nothing compares to the communication made with faces between lovers. I know when my wife is happy, and I know when she is sad and she needs me. Nothing brings me as much joy as seeing her smile at the end of long day of work. ” My own vision became blurry as I felt tears begin to well. 
 
 There was a long silence that I interrupted with a loud sniff from my nose. 
 
 ** “ Very well, human. We have decided you may live, ” ** A sigh escapes my lips. ** “ We will now claim your visual organs to further understand the science behind what you ’ ve said. ” ** 
 
 A very loud whining noise came from a machine behind me. I could feel a breeze on my hair coming from some type of spinning part. I dropped my hands to my lap, and took a look at my wife for the very last time.
text:
I scanned the room in a single, swift glance. My wife lay unconscious just feet from my knees, her wrists and ankles bound by the same faintly glowing restraints that encircled mine. Aside from that eerie luminescence, the chamber was suffocatingly dark. My captors—seated on low stools before me—cast long, distorted shadows across the walls, lit only by the soft radiance of our shackles. Their faces remained indistinct, swallowed by shadow.  

“We have observed your species for nearly a thousand years. You are simple—yet you possess one ability even our highest prophets cannot fathom.”  

Sweat traced cold, salty paths down my temples and into the corners of my mouth. I glanced at my wife—her chest rising and falling steadily.  

“Explain your power of sight.”  

*My* power of sight? Truthfully, it’s been failing for years—I need glasses just to read the newspaper. I’d never considered vision a *power*, let alone something beyond the grasp of an advanced alien civilization.  

“Speak, human—if you wish to live.”  

“Sight,” I began, lifting my gaze and using the dim glow of my wrist restraints to make out the silhouettes before me. “Sight is the gateway to understanding the world. It gives meaning to every other sense. When I move, I trust my steps. When I stand still, I grasp everything around me.”  

I paused—then, prompted by a sharp, impatient grunt:  
“Food tastes richer when I can see it. The most vibrant fruit is usually the juiciest. The brightest-plumaged birds sing the sweetest songs. And whenever I hear a sound, I turn my eyes toward its source…”  
I hesitated again, glancing at my wife—her brown hair splayed across the floor, her face slack with unconsciousness.  
“And nothing compares to the silent language of faces between lovers. I know when she’s happy. I know when she’s sad—and when she needs me. Nothing brings me more joy than seeing her smile at the end of a long day.”  
My vision blurred as tears welled.  

Silence stretched—thick and absolute—until I broke it with a ragged sniff.  

“Very well, human. You may live.”  
A breath escaped me—relief, fleeting and shallow.  
“We will now remove your visual organs to study the science behind what you’ve described.”  

A high-pitched whine erupted from a machine behind me. A cool draft stirred my hair—some unseen rotor spinning faster. I lowered my hands to my lap and looked at my wife one last time.

title: Crop Production and Agricultural Carbon Emissions: Relationship Diagnosis and Decomposition Analysis
human: Modern agriculture contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions, and agriculture has become the second biggest source of carbon emissions in China. In this context, it is necessary for China to study the nexus of agricultural economic growth and carbon emissions. Taking Jilin province as an example, this paper applied the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) hypothesis and a decoupling analysis to examine the relationship between crop production and agricultural carbon emissions during 2000-2018, and it further provided a decomposition analysis of the changes in agricultural carbon emissions using the log mean Divisia index (LMDI) method. The results were as follows: (1) Based on the results of CO2 EKC estimation, an N-shaped EKC was found; in particular, the upward trend in agricultural carbon emissions has not changed recently. (2) According to the results of the decoupling analysis, expansive coupling occurred for 9 years, which was followed by weak decoupling for 5 years, and strong decoupling and strong coupling occurred for 2 years each. There was no stable evolutionary path from coupling to decoupling, and this has remained true recently. (3) We used the LMDI method to decompose the driving factors of agricultural carbon emissions into four factors: the agricultural carbon emission intensity effect, structure effect, economic effect, and labor force effect. From a policymaking perspective, we integrated the results of both the EKC and the decoupling analysis and conducted a detailed decomposition analysis, focusing on several key time points. Agricultural economic growth was found to have played a significant role on many occasions in the increase in agricultural carbon emissions, while agricultural carbon emission intensity was important to the decline in agricultural carbon emissions. Specifically, the four factors' driving direction in the context of agricultural carbon emissions was not stable. We also found that the change in agricultural carbon emissions was affected more by economic policy than by environmental policy. Finally, we put forward policy suggestions for low-carbon agricultural development in Jilin province.
text:
Modern agriculture is a major contributor to global greenhouse gas emissions and, in China, has emerged as the second-largest source of carbon emissions. Against this backdrop, understanding the relationship between agricultural economic growth and carbon emissions is critical for China’s climate mitigation strategy. This study focuses on Jilin Province as a representative case, employing three complementary analytical frameworks—the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis, decoupling analysis, and the Log Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) decomposition method—to investigate the dynamics between crop production and agricultural carbon emissions over the period 2000–2018.

The key findings are as follows:  
(1) EKC estimation reveals an N-shaped curve, indicating that agricultural carbon emissions initially rose with economic growth, declined temporarily at intermediate income levels, but have recently resumed an upward trajectory—suggesting no sustained turning point has yet been reached.  
(2) Decoupling analysis identifies a highly unstable evolution: expansive coupling prevailed for nine years, followed by five years of weak decoupling, and two years each of strong decoupling and strong coupling. Critically, no consistent or progressive transition from coupling toward sustained decoupling has occurred—and this instability persists to date.  
(3) LMDI decomposition attributes changes in agricultural carbon emissions to four drivers: carbon emission intensity, sectoral structure, economic scale (output), and labor force size. The directional influence of each factor proved inconsistent over time. Notably, agricultural economic growth was a dominant driver of emission increases in multiple periods, whereas reductions in carbon emission intensity were the primary contributor to emission declines. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that economic policy levers exerted a stronger influence on emission trends than environmental policy instruments.

Based on these integrated insights, the paper concludes with targeted, evidence-based policy recommendations to advance low-carbon agricultural development in Jilin Province.

title: Causes of vision loss at China's largest blind school during a period of significant economic growth: 2008-2016
human: To investigate the different causes of vision loss and school-based treatment regimens at Quanzhou Blind School (QBS), China's largest blind school, in 2008 and 2016. In 2008, 144 students received comprehensive eye examinations along with a complete family and ophthalmic history; in 2016, 125 students were examined. Vision loss was categorized into visual impairment and blindness classifications based on WHO guidelines. The etiologies of impairment and blindness in 2008 were compared to those in 2016 using the Fisher exact test. The prevalence and type of visual aids were also analyzed during this period. The leading cause of visual impairment significantly shifted from corneal scarring in 2008 to retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) in 2016 (P = 0.020). Congenital cataracts remained the leading cause of blindness in 2008 and 2016. In 2016 there was a significant increase in the use of visual aids, with 63.2% of students using them in 2016 compared to 8.3% in 2008 (P = 0.0001). Between 2008 and 2016, the leading cause of visual impairment shifted from corneal scarring to ROP, while congenital cataracts remained the leading cause of blindness.
text: This study investigated the etiologies of vision loss and school-based management strategies at Quanzhou Blind School (QBS)—China’s largest blind school—in 2008 and 2016. In 2008, 144 students underwent comprehensive ophthalmic examinations, including detailed family and ocular histories; in 2016, 125 students were similarly evaluated. Vision loss was classified as either visual impairment or blindness according to World Health Organization (WHO) criteria. Etiologic distributions for both visual impairment and blindness were compared between the two time points using Fisher’s exact test. The prevalence and types of visual aids used were also assessed. The leading cause of visual impairment shifted significantly from corneal scarring in 2008 to retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) in 2016 (*P* = 0.020). In contrast, congenital cataracts remained the predominant cause of blindness in both years. Notably, the proportion of students using visual aids increased markedly—from 8.3% in 2008 to 63.2% in 2016 (*P* < 0.0001). Thus, between 2008 and 2016, the primary etiology of visual impairment transitioned from corneal scarring to ROP, whereas congenital cataracts continued to account for the largest share of blindness cases.

title: Genome-wide identification of conserved and novel microRNAs in one bud and two tender leaves of tea plant (Camellia sinensis) by small RNA sequencing, microarray-based hybridization and genome survey scaffold sequences
human: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are important for plant growth and responses to environmental stresses via post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression. Tea, which is primarily produced from one bud and two tender leaves of the tea plant (Camellia sinensis), is one of the most popular non-alcoholic beverages worldwide owing to its abundance of secondary metabolites. A large number of miRNAs have been identified in various plants, including non-model species. However, due to the lack of reference genome sequences and/or information of tea plant genome survey scaffold sequences, discovery of miRNAs has been limited in C. sinensis. Using small RNA sequencing, combined with our recently obtained genome survey data, we have identified and analyzed 175 conserved and 83 novel miRNAs mainly in one bud and two tender leaves of the tea plant. Among these, 93 conserved and 18 novel miRNAs were validated using miRNA microarray hybridization. In addition, the expression pattern of 11 conserved and 8 novel miRNAs were validated by stem-loop-qRT-PCR. A total of 716 potential target genes of identified miRNAs were predicted. Further, Gene Ontology (GO) and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis revealed that most of the target genes were primarily involved in stress response and enzymes related to phenylpropanoid biosynthesis. The predicted targets of 4 conserved miRNAs were further validated by 5'RLM-RACE. The predicted target genes of majority of miRNAs encoded enzymes, transcription factors, and functional proteins. The miRNA-target transcription factor gene interactions may provide important clues about the regulatory mechanism of these miRNAs in the tea plant. The data reported in this study will make a huge contribution to knowledge on the potential miRNA regulators of the secondary metabolism pathway and other important biological processes in C. sinensis.

A large number of miRNAs have been identified in various plants, including non-model species. However, due to the lack of reference genome sequences and/or information on tea plant genome survey scaffold sequences, discovery of miRNAs has been limited in C. sinensis. Using small RNA sequencing, combined with our recently obtained genome survey data, we have identified and analyzed 175 conserved and 83 novel miRNAs mainly in one bud and two tender leaves of the tea plant. Among these, 93 conserved and 18 novel miRNAs were validated using miRNA microarray hybridization. In addition, the expression patterns of 11 conserved and 8 novel miRNAs were validated by stem-loop-qRT-PCR. A total of 716 potential target genes of identified miRNAs were predicted. text:
Neuroscience isn’t for everyone—but Backyard Brains co-founder Greg Gage is determined to make it less intimidating and far more accessible.  
Gage believes that advancing fundamental neuroscience research is essential to curing devastating neurological disorders like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s.  
Together with his partner Tim Marzullo, he founded Backyard Brains to demystify brain science—making it engaging and affordable for learners of all ages and socioeconomic backgrounds.  
Using a hands-on, do-it-yourself approach, the company designs low-cost educational kits that bring real neuroscience into classrooms—and even kitchens.  
Gage aims to show students that studying the brain can be exciting, inspiring the next generation of neuroscientists along the way.  
One flagship product, the SpikerBox, enables users to record and stimulate neurons—say, from insects—and visualize the resulting neural activity on smartphones using custom apps.  
His goal? To help children and teens of all ages grasp how brains communicate, one experiment at a time.  
A recent Backyard Brains video—showing squid skin cells responding to an iPod—went viral on YouTube, underscoring how compelling and broadly appealing interactive, visual neuroscience can be.  
By building simple, entry-level tools from off-the-shelf electronics, Backyard Brains seeks to spark curiosity and ignite a “neuro-revolution.”  
Gage spoke with CNN at TED 2012 in Long Beach, California:  

CNN: Why did you start Backyard Brains?  
Gage: We wanted to take cutting-edge, prohibitively expensive neuroscience techniques—and simplify and lower their cost enough to use them in high school, even as early as fifth grade.  

CNN: Why is teaching neuroscience so important?  
Gage: One in five people worldwide—20% of the global population—will be diagnosed with a neurological disorder. Yet when it comes to treating these conditions, we’re still in the dark ages. The only path forward is foundational neuroscience research. By introducing brain science early in education, we can spark genuine interest—and build a pipeline of future scientists. Our kits are designed to get kids excited about the brain, hands-on, so they pursue careers in this field.  

CNN: What’s your long-term vision for Backyard Brains?  
Gage: The SpikerBox is just the beginning. We aim to bring advanced techniques—like optogenetics, pioneered just years ago—into high school labs. Over the next 10 to 15 years, we hope professors will tell us that more applicants arrive at their labs already experienced in neuroscience experiments—or already thinking deeply about the brain. That’s how the “neuro-revolution” begins: by cultivating a new generation of scientists who understand the brain well enough to solve today’s most urgent neurological challenges. We simply need to accelerate the science—to help cure these diseases.  

Brandon Ancil and Richard Galant contributed to this report.

title: Socio-economic disparity in global burden of near vision loss: an analysis for 2017 with time trends since 1990
human: To investigate the socio-economic disparity in global burden of near vision loss by disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs). The DALY numbers of country income groups by World Bank classification and the national age-standardized DALY rates caused by near vision loss were obtained from Global Burden of Disease Study 2017. Human development index (HDI) was collected from the Human Development Report. The association between age-standardized DALY rates and HDI was analysed. Additionally, the concentration index (CI) and the relative index of inequality (RII) were employed to assess the trends of socio-economic disparity in the global burden of near vision loss from 1990 to 2017. The global burden of near vision loss increased from 5.3 million DALYs in 1990 to 9.8 million DALYs in 2017, corresponding to an increase of 82.4%. The highest rate of increase for 1990-2017 occurred in low-income country group (97.7%). Age-standardized DALY rates were inversely correlated with HDI (Standardized β = -0.679, P < 0.001). Lower HDI countries displayed higher age-standardized DALY rates caused by near vision loss. From 1990 to 2017, CI declined from -0.233 to -0.209, and RII increased from 0.149 to 0.247. The total global burden of near vision loss increased greatly in the past few decades, with low-income countries showing the highest growth. The age-standardized burden was higher in countries with lower socio-economic status. Although a declining trend of socio-economic inequalities was observed, the persistence of disparities still highlights the need to provide more eye care services for developing countries.
text:
This study aimed to examine socio-economic disparities in the global burden of near vision loss, measured in disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs). Data on national age-standardized DALY rates and country-level DALY totals—stratified by World Bank income classification—were drawn from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017. The Human Development Index (HDI) was obtained from the United Nations Development Programme’s Human Development Report. We assessed the association between age-standardized DALY rates and HDI using linear regression and quantified trends in socio-economic inequality over time (1990–2017) using the concentration index (CI) and the relative index of inequality (RII).  

Globally, the burden of near vision loss rose substantially—from 5.3 million DALYs in 1990 to 9.8 million DALYs in 2017—an 82.4% increase. The largest proportional rise occurred in low-income countries (97.7%). Age-standardized DALY rates exhibited a strong inverse correlation with HDI (standardized β = −0.679; *P* < 0.001), confirming that lower HDI was consistently associated with higher disease burden. Over the study period, the CI decreased from −0.233 to −0.209, while the RII increased from 0.149 to 0.247—indicating a modest reduction in the magnitude of socio-economic inequality, though disparities remain pronounced.  

These findings underscore a growing global burden of near vision loss, disproportionately concentrated in lower-income and lower-HDI countries. Despite a slight attenuation in inequality over time, persistent disparities highlight an urgent need to strengthen and equitably scale up eye care services—particularly in resource-limited settings.

“It's folly, Rhoda!--the uttermost madness ever conceived! I do not believe--I know that Dahlia would never consent--first, to marry any man but myself; secondly, to marry a man who is not a perfect gentleman. Her delicacy distinguishes her among women.”

“Mr. Blancove, my sister is nearly dead, only that she is so strong. The disgrace has overwhelmed her, it has. When she is married, she will thank and honour him, and see nothing but his love and kindness. I will leave you now.”

He looked up at the name of the street, and shot away from her. Rhoda departed in another direction, firm, since she had seen Sedgett pass, that his nobleness should not meet with an ill reward. She endowed him with fair moral qualities, which she contrasted against Edward Blancove's evil ones; and it was with a democratic fervour of contempt that she dismissed the superior outward attractions of the gentleman.

This neighbourhood was unknown to Edward, and, after plunging about in one direction and another, he found that he had missed his way. Down innumerable dusky streets of dwarfed houses, showing soiled silent window-blinds, he hurried and chafed; at one moment in sharp joy that he had got a resolution, and the next dismayed by the singular petty impediments which were tripping him. “My dearest!” his heart cried to Dahlia, “did I wrong you so? I will make all well. It was the work of a fiend.” Now he turned to right, now to left, and the minutes flew. They flew; and in the gathering heat of his brain he magnified things until the sacrifice of herself Dahlia was preparing for smote his imagination as with a blaze of the upper light, and stood sublime before him in the grandeur of old tragedy. “She has blinded her eyes, stifled her senses, eaten her heart. Oh! my beloved! my wife! my poor girl! and all to be free from shame in her father's sight!” Who could have believed that a girl of Dahlia's class would at once have felt the shame so keenly, and risen to such pure heights of heroism? The sacrifice flouted conception; it mocked the steady morning. He refused to believe in it, but the short throbs of his blood were wiser.

A whistling urchin became his guide. The little lad was carelessly giving note to a popular opera tune, with happy disregard of concord. It chanced that the tune was one which had taken Dahlia's ear, and, remembering it and her pretty humming of it in the old days, Edward's wrestling unbelief with the fatality of the hour sank, so entirely was he under the sovereignty of his sensations. He gave the boy a big fee, desiring superstitiously to feel that one human creature could bless the hour. The house was in view. He knocked, and there came a strange murmur of some denial. “She is here,” he said, menacingly.

The landlady begged him to wait; but to sit and see the minutes--the black emissaries of perdition--fly upon their business, was torture as big as to endure the tearing off of his flesh till the skeleton stood out. Up to this point he had blamed himself; now he accused the just heavens. Yea! is not a sinner their lawful quarry? and do they not slip the hounds with savage glee, and hunt him down from wrong to evil, from evil to infamy, from infamy to death, from death to woe everlasting? And is this their righteousness?--He caught at the rusty garden rails to steady his feet.

Algernon was employed in the comfortable degustation of his breakfast, meditating whether he should transfer a further slice of ham or of Yorkshire pie to his plate, or else have done with feeding and light a cigar, when Edward appeared before him.

Don't talk to me on any other subject,

One of five prisoners receiving treatment for a suspected case of Ebola virus in Uganda escaped overnight Friday from the hospital at the center of the outbreak, a health official said.
"Should his results come back and he is positive, that causes us a lot of worry.
So right now, we have resolved that the remaining prisoners will be cuffed on the beds for fear that they might also escape," said Dr.
Jackson Amune, commissioner at the Ministry of Health.
The inmates from Kibaale prison are among 30 people at Kagadi hospital with suspected cases of the virus.
Two additional patients have confirmed cases, according to Doctors Without Borders.
The prisoners have been showing Ebola-like symptoms of vomiting, diarrhea and fever, Dr.
Dan Kyamanywa said Thursday.
"We do expect the number of suspected cases to increase,"
Kyamanywa said.
"It's important to break transmission and reduce the number of contacts that suspected cases have."
Read more: Ebola outbreak suspected among Uganda prisoners .
Many patients fled Kagadi hospital when Ebola was confirmed, he said, and the facility is struggling to respond to all the call-outs to suspected cases. The outbreak began in the Kibaale district in western Uganda with 53 confirmed cases. At least 16 people have died. An additional 312 people have suspected cases of the virus and have been isolated, pending further testing. The deaths have stoked heightened fear of the virus, a highly infectious, often fatal agent spread through direct contact with bodily fluids. Symptoms can include fever, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, a measles-like rash, red eyes and, at times, bleeding from body openings. "I would like to stress that the disease is under control," said Joaquim Saweka, the World Health Organization representative to Uganda. Health officials urged the public to report any suspected cases, to avoid contact with anyone infected and to wear gloves and masks while disinfecting bedding and clothing of infected people. Officials also advised avoiding public gatherings in the affected district. Read more: Could the Ebola outbreak spread to the U.S.? Teams in Uganda are taking an aggressive approach, including trying to track down anyone who came into contact with patients infected with the virus, and health workers have been gearing up to protect themselves and deal with an influx of cases. The workers include people from Uganda's Ministry of Health, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the World Health Organization. Meanwhile, officials in Kenya were taking extra precautions after at least two patients showed symptoms of the virus, according to Jackstone Omoto, a medical official in Siaya, western Kenya. One man tested negative. A second man and two relatives have been isolated at the Moi Teaching & Referral Hospital in Eldoret, pending test results. The man was traveling from South Sudan to Kenya through Uganda. "We are tracing the bus that he (traveled on), and we have requested the company to contact the ministry so we can know who else was in the bus," said Beth Mugo, public health minister. The Ebola virus was first detected in 1976 in the central African nation of Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo). The virus is named after a river in that country. There are five strains of the virus, all named after the areas where they were found: Zaire, Sudan, Cote d'Ivoire, Bundibugyo and Reston, according to the WHO. CNN's Lillian Leposo and Aliza Kassim contributed to this report.

title: COP21 Roadmap: Do innovation, financial development, and transportation infrastructure matter for environmental sustainability in China?
human: The purpose of the present study is to explain the long-run and causal effects of innovation, financial development, and transportation infrastructure on CO2 emissions using the combined cointegration and wavelet coherence approaches over the period from 1971 to 2018, while using economic growth as a control variable in the model. The outcomes of the Bayer-Hanck cointegration test show that there is an important cointegration equation among CO2 emissions, innovation, financial development, transportation infrastructure, and real GDP. Moreover, the findings from a wavelet power spectrum reveal that there is a significant vulnerability in innovation, financial development, transportation infrastructure, and CO2 emissions at different time frames and frequencies. Furthermore, the outcomes of wavelet coherence approach reveal that (i) Innovation is observed as a significant predictor of CO2 emissions over the period from 2007 to 2013; (ii) In the long run, there are negative correlations between CO2 emissions and financial development; (iii) Over the periods from 2000 to 2015, and from 1985 to 1989, transportation significantly causes CO2 emissions. Our findings have substantial policy implications that suggest there is a need to strengthen innovation and transportation infrastructure to achieve environmental sustainability targets.
text: This study investigates the long-run and causal relationships between innovation, financial development, transportation infrastructure, and CO₂ emissions over 1971–2018, employing a combined cointegration and wavelet coherence framework—with real GDP included as a control variable. Bayer–Hanck cointegration tests confirm a robust long-run equilibrium relationship among CO₂ emissions, innovation, financial development, transportation infrastructure, and real GDP. Wavelet power spectrum analysis further reveals pronounced time–frequency variability in all four explanatory variables and CO₂ emissions. Wavelet coherence results indicate that: (i) innovation significantly predicts CO₂ emissions during 2007–2013; (ii) financial development exhibits a persistent negative association with CO₂ emissions in the long run; and (iii) transportation infrastructure exerts a statistically significant causal effect on CO₂ emissions during 1985–1989 and 2000–2015. These findings carry important policy implications: strengthening innovation capacity and upgrading sustainable transportation infrastructure are critical for advancing environmental sustainability goals.

title: Synthesis and characterization of a hyperbranched grafting copolymer PEI-g-PLeu for gene and drug co-delivery
human: L-Leucine (Leu) is a hydrophobic natural amino acid and can polymerize into poly-L-Leucine (PLeu) to be an excellent biocompatible material. In this paper, a hyperbranched copolymer polyethyleneimine-g-poly-L-leucine (PEI-g-PLeu) was synthesized by ring-opening polymerization with leucine NCA as monomer and PEI as initiator, which will be used as drug and gene co-delivery system for cancer therapy. To characterize the transfection efficiency in vitro, pGL3 as the reporter gene was loaded in PEI-g-PLeu to form complexes. Doxorubicin (DOX) with cis-aconitic anhydride linker (CAD) and calf thymus DNA (as model DNA) were co-loaded in PEI-g-PLeu to obtain PEI-g-PLeu/DNA/CAD nanoparticles to measure Zeta potentials and particle sizes. Lastly, CAD and modified Bc12-shRNA(as therapeutic gene) were co-loaded in PEI-g-PLeu to get PEI-g-PLeu/CAD/DNA complexes. Our finding revealed when PEI and PLeu with the molar ratio of 1:240, and PEI-g-PLeu and DNA with the mass ratio of 1:5, PEI-g-PLeu/CAD/DNA had negligible cytotoxicity with equivalent gene transfaction efficiency compared with PEI25k. As a result, PEI-g-PLeu/CAD/DNA was a promising drug and gene co-delivery system.
text:
L-Leucine (Leu) is a naturally occurring, hydrophobic amino acid that can be polymerized into poly-L-leucine (PLeu), a biocompatible material with favorable properties for biomedical applications. In this study, we synthesized a hyperbranched copolymer—polyethyleneimine-graft-poly-L-leucine (PEI-g-PLeu)—via ring-opening polymerization using leucine N-carboxyanhydride (Leu-NCA) as the monomer and branched polyethyleneimine (PEI) as the macroinitiator. This copolymer was developed as a dual-functional carrier for the co-delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs and therapeutic nucleic acids in cancer therapy.

To evaluate its gene delivery performance *in vitro*, PEI-g-PLeu was complexed with the luciferase reporter plasmid pGL3. For physicochemical characterization—including zeta potential and hydrodynamic particle size measurements—PEI-g-PLeu was co-formulated with calf thymus DNA (as a model plasmid) and doxorubicin (DOX) conjugated via a cis-aconitic anhydride (CAD) linker, yielding PEI-g-PLeu/DNA/CAD nanoparticles. Finally, to assess therapeutic efficacy, PEI-g-PLeu was co-loaded with CAD-conjugated DOX and Bcl-2-targeting short hairpin RNA (Bcl-2-shRNA), generating PEI-g-PLeu/CAD/shRNA complexes.

Our results demonstrate that at a Leu:PEI molar ratio of 240:1 in the copolymer synthesis, and a PEI-g-PLeu:DNA mass ratio of 1:5 in complex formation, the resulting PEI-g-PLeu/CAD/shRNA complexes exhibit negligible cytotoxicity while achieving transfection efficiency comparable to that of the gold-standard 25 kDa PEI (PEI25k). These findings establish PEI-g-PLeu/CAD/shRNA as a highly promising platform for combined chemotherapy and gene therapy in oncology.

title: Nanomechanical characterization of time-dependent deformation/recovery on human dentin caused by radiation-induced glycation
human: An increase in non-enzymatic collagen matrix cross-links, such as advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), is known to be a major complication in human mineralized tissues, often causing abnormal fractures. However, degradation of mechanical properties in relation to AGEs has not been fully elucidated at the material level. Here, we report nanoscale time-dependent deformation and dimensional recovery of human tooth dentin that has undergone glycation induced by x-ray irradiation. The reduction in enzymatic collagen cross-linking and the increased level of AGEs with concomitant growth of disordered collagen matrix diminished creep deformation recovery in the lower mineralized target region. However, the elevated AGEs level alone did not cause a reduction in time-dependent deformation and its recovery in the higher mineralized target region. In addition to the elevated AGEs level, the degradation of the mechanical properties of mineralized tissues should be assessed with care in respect to multiple parameters in the collagen matrix at the molecular level.
text: An accumulation of non-enzymatic collagen matrix cross-links—particularly advanced glycation end-products (AGEs)—is a well-established contributor to pathological fragility in human mineralized tissues, often leading to atypical fractures. Yet, the mechanistic link between AGE accumulation and the degradation of mechanical properties remains incompletely understood at the material level. Here, we report nanoscale, time-dependent deformation and dimensional recovery behavior in human tooth dentin subjected to glycation induced by X-ray irradiation. In the less mineralized regions, reduced enzymatic collagen cross-linking, elevated AGE levels, and concomitant disruption of collagen matrix organization collectively impaired creep deformation recovery. In contrast, in the more highly mineralized regions, elevated AGE levels alone did not significantly affect time-dependent deformation or its recovery. These findings underscore that, beyond AGE accumulation, assessing the mechanical degradation of mineralized tissues requires careful, multi-parameter evaluation of the collagen matrix at the molecular level.

title: Patch test practices and perceptions of Chinese dermatologists: results of a cross-sectional survey
human: Patch testing is the most valuable tool for diagnosing allergic contact dermatitis. Whereas previous surveys have evaluated patch test practices and perceptions of dermatologists worldwide, no such information is available relating to Chinese dermatologists. We surveyed Chinese dermatologists by using questionnaires to investigate their patch test practices and the prevalence of patch testing. A cross-sectional survey of Chinese dermatologists was conducted at the National Congress of Dermatology in December 2006. Of the 1116 questionnaires distributed, 1089 (97.6%) were returned. Eighty-six per cent of dermatologists reported performing patch testing. Dermatologists from regional hospitals were significantly more likely to perform patch testing (p < 0.001). The majority (80.8%) used the baseline (standard) allergen series made in China. Eighty-seven per cent of testers performed only a single patch test reading. The dermatologists' perceptions of the patch test indicated that 43.1% of the respondents thought that patch testing could be used to diagnose irritant contact dermatitis, and only 30.3% of the respondents made the correct choice when asked to read a patch test reaction. Patch testing is widespread among Chinese dermatologists, but further improvement and education regarding the procedure is required.

title: Tomato Anomalies Detection in Greenhouse Scenarios Based on YOLO-Dense
human: Greenhouse cultivation can improve crop yield and quality, and it not only solves people's daily needs but also brings considerable gains to the agricultural staff. One of the most widely cultivated greenhouse crops is tomato, mainly because of its high nutritional value and its good taste. However, there are a number of anomalies for the tomato crop that pose a threat for its greenhouse cultivation. Detection of tomato anomalies in the complex natural environment is an important research direction in the field of plant science. Automated identification of tomato anomalies is still a challenging task because of its small size and complex background. To solve the problem of tomato anomaly detection in the complex natural environment, a novel YOLO-Dense was proposed based on a one-stage deep detection YOLO framework. By adding a dense connection module in the network architecture, the network inference speed of the proposed model can be effectively improved. By using the K-means algorithm to cluster the anchor box, nine different sizes of anchor boxes with potential objects to be identified were obtained. The multiscale training strategy was adopted to improve the recognition accuracy of objects at different scales. The experimental results show that the mAP and detection time of a single image of the YOLO-Dense network is 96.41% and 20.28 ms, respectively. Compared with SSD, Faster R-CNN, and the original YOLOv3 network, the YOLO-Dense model achieved the best performance in tomato anomaly detection under a complex natural environment.
text: Greenhouse cultivation enhances both crop yield and quality, meeting daily food demands while generating significant income for agricultural workers. Among greenhouse-grown crops, tomatoes are among the most widely cultivated—valued for their high nutritional content and excellent flavor. However, tomato crops are susceptible to various anomalies that threaten greenhouse production. Detecting these anomalies in complex natural environments is a key research focus in plant science. Automated anomaly detection remains challenging due to the small size of tomato defects and the cluttered, variable backgrounds typical of greenhouse settings. To address this, we propose YOLO-Dense—a novel one-stage deep detection model built upon the YOLO framework. It incorporates a dense connection module to accelerate network inference without sacrificing accuracy. Anchor boxes were optimized using K-means clustering, yielding nine size-tuned anchors aligned with common anomaly shapes. A multiscale training strategy further improves detection robustness across varying object sizes. Experiments show that YOLO-Dense achieves a mean average precision (mAP) of 96.41% and processes each image in just 20.28 ms. Compared to SSD, Faster R-CNN, and the original YOLOv3, YOLO-Dense delivers superior performance for tomato anomaly detection in complex natural environments.

`` Excuse me?'' 
 
 Startled, you look up; the local newspaper was boring you anyway. `` Can I help you?'' 
 
 `` Yeah, I saw you reading, I wondered if you might be from'round here?'' The man shrugs, seemingly rising up and sinking back into a slump, as if also bored, `` I'm kinda lost...'' His gaze shifts around, almost awkwardly, as if your eye contact is the last thing he wants. Come to think of it, he does seem to be acting strangely - jumpy, almost scared, as if the leaves collecting in piles at the sides of the road might suddenly blow away and reveal a great fear of his. But you cast this away: it's probably nothing, you think. Some people are just twitchy, he surely has no ill intent. 
 
 `` I'm from around here, where do you need directions to?'' 
 
 He thrusts his hand into his pocket and eventually pulls out a crumpled map covered in nondescript markings. `` Here.'' He points to an area circled vividly in red pen. You get up, and upon discovering the map is help upside down rotate your head awkwardly in order to read the street name - but suddenly, you stop. It's your road. `` Which house did you want?'' `` Number 32, I think.'' 
 
 The breath catches in your throat. You ask why he needs to go there - you were n't aware of anything being delivered at all, but if it was a delivery guy he was n't in uniform so that was n't it. Had she - your wife, that is - finally given up? You'd been going through tough times recently, but surely it had n't come to this. So you think. `` Excuse me?'' Once again, the man standing in front of you interrupts your train of thought. Once again, you look up, and see his eyes darting wildly. No, that ca n't be it. The kids are at home sleeping, and your wife, your oh so beloved wife, will be watching TV and looking after your baby, the third, a girl. `` Sorry, I need to go, I ca n't help you,'' you stumble out a reply as you grab what little you had with you and make a start. 
 
 `` Wait!'' 
 
 You turn one final time, to see the man, panicking, frantically scream, `` I'm sorry! They made me, I did n't want it to be this way!'' 
 
 And then he falls, as if all his life had been sucked out and all that was left was a lifeless sack of meat. 
 
 You turn back around, ready to sprint home. And there's another man, standing there. A pistol gripped firmly in his hand. You wonder to yourself, why did n't I hear the shot? And then you look down, and notice the steam of blood slowly dripping from the exit wound in your chest. Funny, you think, that this is how it ends, dying in the street after all that time you'd spent in the military - you could have gotten killed at any point then, but it happens when you're safe at home. 
 
 You look back up. 
 
 You hear two dull thuds, and then the world tips sideways. The last thing to go through your mind - before the final bullet, that is - was to think, to wish, that you'd gotten home sooner to make it up to your wife. And then, the flowers you bought for her, now stained and splattered in crimson mist, fall out of your lifeless hand. 
 
 ``... Excuse me?''

text:
“Excuse me?”  

Startled, you look up—the local paper had been dulling your senses anyway. “Can I help you?”  

“Yeah—I saw you reading. Figured you might be from ’round here?” The man shrugs, as if rising slightly only to slump back into himself, his posture betraying the same restlessness that clouds his voice. “I’m kinda lost…” His gaze skitters away—everywhere but at you—as though your attention is the last thing he wants. Come to think of it, he *does* seem off: jumpy, almost frightened, as if the dry leaves piling along the roadside might scatter at any moment and expose some deep, hidden dread. But you dismiss it. Probably nothing. Some people just fidget; he surely means no harm.  

“I’m from around here—where do you need directions?”  

He digs a hand into his pocket and pulls out a crumpled map, its surface smudged with vague, indecipherable markings. “Here.” He taps a spot circled boldly in red ink. You stand, tilt your head awkwardly to read the street name—upside down, as it turns out—and then freeze. It’s *your* street.  

“Which house were you looking for?”  
“Number thirty-two, I think.”  

Your breath hitches. You ask why he needs to go there—you hadn’t heard about any deliveries, and if he were a courier, he’s wearing no uniform. Had *she*—your wife, that is—finally given up? Things had been strained lately, yes—but surely it hadn’t come to this. Or so you tell yourself.  

“Excuse me?”  
Again, the man interrupts your thoughts. Again, you look up—and catch his eyes darting wildly. No. That can’t be it. The kids are asleep at home. Your wife—your beloved, steadfast wife—is watching TV, holding your third child, a baby girl.  

“Sorry—I need to go. I can’t help you.” The words tumble out as you snatch up your things and step away.  

“Wait!”  

You turn one last time—to see him unraveling: panicked, frantic, shouting, “I’m sorry! They made me—I didn’t want it to be like this!”  

Then he collapses—not like someone falling, but like something deflating: all life suddenly drained, leaving behind only a hollow, lifeless weight.  

You pivot, ready to sprint home—and there he is. Another man. A pistol held steady in his grip.  

*Why didn’t I hear the shot?*  
Then you glance down—and see it: crimson steam rising faintly from the exit wound in your chest.  

Funny, you think, how it ends like this—dying on a quiet street, after all those years in the military. You could’ve died at any moment back then. But not here. Not now. Not when you thought you were safe at home.  

You lift your eyes.  

Two muffled thuds. Then the world tilts sideways.  

The last thing that crosses your mind—before the final bullet strikes—is not fear, not anger, but a raw, aching wish: *If only I’d gotten home sooner. If only I’d made it up to her.*  

And as your fingers go slack, the flowers you bought for her—now streaked and splattered with crimson mist—slip from your hand and fall to the pavement.  

“…Excuse me?”  

You look up from your newspaper—you’d nearly forgotten the nervous man standing before you.

title: TCM-Blast for traditional Chinese medicine genome alignment with integrated resources
human: The traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) genome project aims to reveal the genetic information and regulatory network of herbal medicines, and to clarify their molecular mechanisms in the prevention and treatment of human diseases. Moreover, the TCM genome could provide the basis for the discovery of the functional genes of active ingredients in TCM, and for the breeding and improvement of TCM. The traditional Chinese Medicine Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (TCM-Blast) is a web interface for TCM protein and DNA sequence similarity searches. It contains approximately 40G of genome data on TCMs, including protein and DNA sequence for 36 TCMs with high medical value.The development of a publicly accessible TCM genome alignment database hosted on the TCM-Blast website ( http://viroblast.pungentdb.org.cn/TCM-Blast/viroblast.php ) has expanded to query multiple sequence databases to obtain TCM genome data, and provide user-friendly output for easy analysis and browsing of BLAST results. The genome sequencing of TCMs helps to elucidate the biosynthetic pathways of important secondary metabolites and provides an essential resource for gene discovery studies and molecular breeding. The TCMs genome provides a valuable resource for the investigation of novel bioactive compounds and drugs from these TCMs under the guidance of TCM clinical practice. Our database could be expanded to other TCMs after the determination of their genome data.

text:
“Contemporary Issues in Organizations” by Marianne Tracy (Critical Essay)  

This essay, authored by organizational consultant and coach Marianne Tracy, centers on insights from Manfred Kets de Vries—a distinguished Dutch scholar, psychoanalyst, and leadership expert who integrates psychoanalytic theory with economics in his work on organizational leadership (Vries, 1993). The piece is based on an interview Tracy conducted with Kets de Vries, focusing on the psychological underpinnings of leadership in contemporary organizations.  

The essay opens with Kets de Vries’ perspective on truth, deception, and leadership. He observes that humans are inherently prone to lying—not out of malice, but as a means of asserting autonomy and safeguarding personal boundaries. Within organizations, fear—particularly of authority—often drives individuals to misrepresent reality in order to appease superiors. Tracy notes that Kets de Vries traces this tendency to early family dynamics (Tracy, 2004), citing how caregivers, such as mothers, may inadvertently teach children to suppress authentic emotions to maintain harmony. The essay then examines how external consultants can help disrupt entrenched patterns of organizational dishonesty and identifies structural factors—such as hierarchical rigidity and performance pressures—that foster deceit. It further considers the role of business schools in cultivating integrity, highlighting Kets de Vries’ view that core ethical values are largely formed before university; thus, business education has limited capacity to reshape moral character. The essay concludes by underscoring the persistent difficulty junior staff face in speaking truthfully to those in power.  

The article offers valuable, psychologically grounded insights into organizational leadership. Its most compelling contribution lies in framing honesty—and dishonesty—as deeply rooted in human development and relational dynamics. For instance, it presents lying not merely as unethical behavior but as a “sign of independence” (Tracy, 2004), offering a nuanced lens for interpreting workplace conduct. Equally provocative is Kets de Vries’ comparison of organizational life to the psychological conditions of a concentration camp—an initially jarring analogy that, upon explanation, illuminates how power imbalances, surveillance, and existential threat can erode authenticity in institutional settings.  

As an interview-based essay, its structure reflects Tracy’s editorial judgment and interpretive skill. She organizes the material coherently, uses clear subheadings to guide readers through Kets de Vries’ arguments, and translates his complex, interdisciplinary ideas into accessible language—enhancing readability and comprehension.  

That said, the essay relies heavily on illustrative anecdotes, some of which dilute its scholarly rigor. While these narratives may resonate with practitioners, they risk undermining academic credibility and limiting appeal to leadership scholars seeking theoretically robust or empirically anchored analysis.  

Overall, Tracy’s essay provides a thoughtful, accessible interpretation of Kets de Vries’ ideas on honesty in organizations. Though its tone leans informal and its evidence anecdotal, it effectively conveys key psychological insights relevant to leaders at all levels—from newcomers navigating hierarchy to senior executives shaping organizational culture.  

References  
Tracy, M. 2004, ‘Contemporary issues in organizations’, *Development and Learning in Organizations*, vol. 18, no. 6, pp. 4–6.  
Vries, M. K. de 1993, *Leaders, Fools, and Impostors: Essays on the Psychology of Leadership*, Jossey-Bass.

title: Lignocellulosic crop residue composting by cellulolytic nitrogen-fixing bacteria: A novel tool for environmental sustainability
human: Lignocellulosic crop residue (LCCR) composting is a cost-effective and sustainable approach for addressing environmental pollution associated with open biomass burning and application of chemical fertilizers in agriculture. The value-added bio-product of the composting process contributes to the improvement of the soil properties and plant growth in an environment-friendly way. However, the conventional process employed for composting LCCRs is slow and becomes an impediment for farmers who plant two or three crops a year. This concern has led to the development of different techniques for rapid composting of LCCRs. The use of cellulolytic nitrogen-fixing microorganisms for composting has emerged as a promising method for enhancing LCCR composting and quality of the compost. Therefore, this review addresses the recent progress on the potential use of cellulolytic nitrogen-fixing bacteria (CNFB) for LCCR composting and discusses various applications of nutrient-rich compost for sustainable agriculture to increase crop yields in a nature-friendly way. This knowledge of bacteria with both cellulose-degrading and nitrogen-fixing activities is significant with respect to rapid composting, soil fertility, plant growth and sustainable management of the lignocellulosic agricultural waste and it provides a means for the development of new technology for sustainability.
text: Lignocellulosic crop residue (LCCR) composting offers a cost-effective and environmentally sustainable solution to two major agricultural challenges: the environmental hazards of open-field biomass burning and the overreliance on synthetic fertilizers. The resulting nutrient-rich compost enhances soil structure, fertility, and plant growth while minimizing ecological impact. However, conventional LCCR composting is inherently slow—often requiring several months—posing a significant constraint for farmers practicing intensive cropping systems with two or three harvests per year. To overcome this limitation, rapid composting technologies have been actively developed and refined. Among these, the application of cellulolytic nitrogen-fixing bacteria (CNFB) has emerged as a particularly promising strategy: these microbes simultaneously accelerate lignocellulose degradation and enrich compost with biologically fixed nitrogen, thereby improving both composting efficiency and final product quality. This review synthesizes recent advances in the use of CNFB for LCCR composting and explores the multifaceted applications of the resulting high-quality compost in sustainable agriculture—including enhanced crop productivity, improved soil health, and reduced environmental footprint. Critically, CNFB represent a dual-function microbial resource whose integration into composting systems supports rapid waste transformation, long-term soil fertility enhancement, robust plant growth, and the sustainable management of lignocellulosic agricultural residues—laying a scientific foundation for next-generation, nature-based technologies in circular agriculture.

text:
“Sir, the crotch rocket isn’t moving.”  

*Damn speeders.*  

“Make him move—or I’ll plant a bumper sticker on their rear.”  
I’d been a Captain for years, but freight talk remained the only real language—blunt, unvarnished, and utterly indispensable. It was the Luna Lite of Sol slang: crude, efficient, and forged in the long, silent hauls of an industry that prided itself on grit over grace.  

Pilot Heins grinned. “Aye, sending it to the scrap wagon, sir.”  

Like Luna Lite itself, you’d sooner be caught dead than use it—unless you were a freighter. And even then, you drank it ironically. New, wide-eyed spacers at a watering station would point to a boisterous table of denim-clad giants and ask, *What are they drinking?*  

Two rules were drilled into them on Day One—floating in zero-G or not:  
One: Things are never quite what they seem.  
Two: Those who don’t know Rule One get taken advantage of—repeatedly.  

“Send ’em some waves first.”  
No point shaving another week off the Jupiter run if we ended up docked for collateral damage. The watering hole was close—but so was our deadline.  

Freighters were the de facto professors of Spaceway Law 101—much to the chagrin of every fresh spacer who crossed their path. Their lessons stuck. The giants laughed louder. They grew rowdier. They ordered more Luna Lite.  

No one knew the stellar roads like they did. Their casual disregard for grammar, punctuality, and personal space kept it that way.  

“Nothing, sir,” Heins said.  

“Fine. Let’s throw the hammer down.”  
I gripped the armrests. *Their loss.* “Light ’em up!”  

“Aye—banging Rhythm A!”  

His pilot fired ignition. *Cheerful Tune* lurched forward. Everyone felt the engine surge—syncopated, insistent—in Rhythm A. We’d need Rhythm C before the freighter could truly make headway. For now, the judder and sputter were tolerated.  

“Rhythm B!”  

I released the armrests and leaned back. This was routine. Any casualties from the crotch rocket would be chalked up to Rule Three.  

*No regr—*  

Light erupted from the speeder—a searing cone sweeping over *Cheerful Tune*. What had been open void and station flank moments before now shimmered through thin, web-like distortions.  

*Oh shit. A Dry Box? This close to a station?*  

“Rhythm C!”  

*Cheerful Tune* tore through the cone—but remnants clung to the hull like static frost. It had been damned close.  

Heins and I exchanged hollow, sickened glances.  
“If we’d been a second later…”  

“Enough.” I cut him off sharply. We’d have been netted—God knows where.  

“If any of the crew ask, it was *Cheerful Tune* putting on a light show with our new engine modulation. Nothing more.”  

Heins left his console and headed for the lock to First Deck. “Aye, sir,” he replied—and launched down the corridor to tell his mates something entirely different.  

I stayed seated, wondering how soon I could log the incident. The company needed to know. As for managing a crew who’d just narrowly avoided being Dry Boxed—and who knew it—that would have to wait until morning.  

They’d be restless. But I’d earned tomorrow’s trouble.  

I’d failed to follow Rule One.

title: Traditional Chinese medicine for irritable bowel syndrome: A protocol for meta-analysis
human: Irritable bowel syndrom (IBS) is a common functional gastrointestinal disorder which is characterized as recurrent abdominal pain, abdominal discomfort, and abnormal bowel habits such as diarrhea, constipation, both or alternate appear. Although IBS is not fatal, it seriously affects the patients' daily life and work. Western drug, such as antidiarrheals, gastrointestinal antispasmodic, often cannot get satisfying curative effects. However, the therapeutic effect of Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) on IBS is very satisfactory which was shown in a large number of randomized controlled trials. Although TCM has been widely used in clinical practice, its relative effectiveness and safety have not been confirmed. Therefore, this study will use meta-analysis to verify the efficacy and safety of different types of TCM in the treatment of IBS. We search the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Database, Chinese Science and Technology Periodical Database, Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, Pubmed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane library for all randomized controlled trial of TCM for the treatment of IBS from their inception to Oct 15, 2020. Two authors will independently select studies, extract data based on predesigned inclusion and exclusion criteria. Methodological quality assessment and risk of bias will be assessed using Cochrane bias risk tool. All data analysis will be conducted using Revman5.3, WinBUGS 1.4.3, and Stata14.2 software. This study will compare the different outcome indicators of various studies directly and indirectly, and provide a high-quality synthesis of effectiveness and safety of different TCM methods for patients with IBS. The main outcome indicators include effectiveness, remission rate (no drug symptoms), relapse rate, clinical absolute score, and relative score. Secondary outcome indicators included related adverse reactions and serum serotonin concentration. The conclusion of this systematic review will provide a high-quality evidence based on the efficacy and safety of different TCM treatment methods for IBS. This study protocol has been funded through a protocol registry. The registry number is INPLASY2020100052.

title: Fertilizer overuse in Chinese smallholders due to lack of fixed inputs
human: Fertilizer overuse by smallholder farmers is widespread in China, leading to significant financial losses and threatening the environment. Understanding what mechanism behind this is critical for agricultural and environmental sustainability. By using a fixed effect panel model of over 20,000 rural households in China from 1995 to 2016, we found that the low ratio of fixed inputs such as machinery and knowledge to total inputs is the key factor leading to over-fertilization in smallholder farms. Low fixed input can result in or interact with nutrient-unbalanced fertilization, low agricultural income ratio and more cash crops that further aggravate fertilizer overuse. Smallholders lack fixed inputs, then compensate by over-applying fertilizer to attempt to achieve their yield goals. Thus, improving fixed input via increasing the average farm size to 3.8 ha or advanced service rental could save not only 45% fertilizers but also increase 16% agricultural net profit, benefiting agricultural and environmental sustainability.
text: Fertilizer overuse by smallholder farmers is widespread in China, causing substantial financial losses and posing serious environmental risks. Identifying the underlying drivers is critical for advancing agricultural and environmental sustainability. Using a fixed-effects panel model covering over 20,000 rural households from 1995 to 2016, we find that a low ratio of fixed inputs—such as machinery and agronomic knowledge—to total inputs is the primary driver of over-fertilization on smallholder farms. This shortfall in fixed inputs interacts with or exacerbates nutrient-imbalanced fertilization, low agricultural income shares, and higher cultivation of cash crops—all of which further intensify fertilizer overuse. Lacking access to machinery and technical knowledge, smallholders compensate by applying excessive fertilizer in pursuit of yield targets. Consequently, boosting fixed inputs—through either expanding average farm size to 3.8 hectares or scaling up advanced service rental systems—could reduce fertilizer use by 45% while increasing agricultural net profit by 16%, thereby supporting both economic viability and environmental sustainability.

text:
Timothy John “TJ” Brewer, 33, a sheriff’s deputy from Moab, Utah, appeared before the Utah Peace Officer Standards and Training (POST) Council on Wednesday for a disciplinary hearing stemming from a violent incident that occurred on July 11 of last year. Following the hearing, the Council voted 6–5 to suspend Brewer from law enforcement for four years—rejecting the recommended revocation of his certification, but allowing him to retain it by the narrowest possible margin.

The incident unfolded after Brewer hosted his father, Wesley “Corky” Brewer—a respected local fire chief—for dinner. According to police reports, Brewer prepared the meal for himself, his wife Logan, and his father. After Logan went upstairs to put one of their children to bed and failed to return, Brewer followed and allegedly discovered her engaged in sexual activity with his father on their young son’s bed. In response, Brewer physically assaulted his father. Logan fled to her parents’ home, and Wesley returned to his own residence intending to retrieve a firearm. When his wife, Cindy Brewer, attempted to conceal the weapon in their vehicle, Wesley allegedly retrieved a butcher knife and stabbed himself twice—puncturing a lung and lacerating his liver. He was rushed to Moab Regional Hospital and later airlifted to a Colorado hospital for emergency surgery.

Later that same day, Brewer—intoxicated, shirtless, and barefoot—went to the hospital with the stated intent to “kill” his father. In the parking lot, he was initially confronted by his uncle, Curt Brewer, also a sheriff’s deputy. Upon arrival, responding officers reported that TJ repeatedly declared he wanted to kill his father and demanded access to a firearm to “finish the job.” During this confrontation, he also struck an officer attempting to prevent him from entering the hospital.

In the criminal case, Brewer pleaded guilty to two misdemeanor charges: assault and assault on a peace officer. He was sentenced to 24 months’ probation.

At the POST hearing, Brewer expressed profound remorse, stating, “I regret it every day since this incident happened, when I walked upstairs and saw what I saw,” and described the day as “the second-worst day of my life.” He requested a suspension rather than revocation, emphasizing his desire to remain in law enforcement.

Summit County Sheriff Dave Edmunds, a POST Council member, acknowledged the emotional gravity of the initial discovery, commenting, “There’s no doubt in my mind that his actions at the house that day were justified. I believe that practically anybody would have done similarly at the house. Where Mr. Brewer loses me is when he goes back to the hospital.”

Under the terms of his suspension, Brewer will be required to successfully complete the full police academy curriculum again before he may seek reemployment as a sworn peace officer in Utah.

The Brewer family includes multiple law enforcement professionals—spanning sheriff’s deputies, police officers, and firefighters—underscoring the profound personal and professional ramifications of the incident.

title: Effects of xylitol and stevioside on the physical and rheological properties of gelatin from cod skin
human: Jelly and confectionery products are high in sugar and calories. Xylitol and stevioside are natural low-calorie sweeteners and they can be used as an alternative; however, their effects on fish gelatin are unknown. The gelatin was extracted from cod skins and added to xylitol or stevioside (0, 2, 6, 10, 14, and 20% (w/v)) to form gel products. This paper investigated how xylitol and stevioside affected the physical and rheological behaviors of fish gelatin, such as color, gel strength, texture profile analysis, storage modulus (G'), loss modulus (G″), and viscosity. Results showed that the change of color and viscosity in gel products were similar when various concentrations of xylitol or stevioside were added to the fish gelatin. But the effects of xylitol/stevioside on texture profile analysis and G', G″ were different, which might due to the structure variation in xylitol and stevioside. The linear structure of xylitol resulted in ionic interaction, hydrogen bonding, van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic association between xylitol and fish gelatin. Therefore, xylitol is a promising sweetener substitute, which was probably related to its greater solubility and number of -OH groups.
text: Jelly and confectionery products are typically high in sugar and caloric content. Natural, low-calorie sweeteners such as xylitol and stevioside offer promising alternatives; however, their impact on fish gelatin functionality remains poorly understood. In this study, gelatin was extracted from Atlantic cod skins and incorporated with either xylitol or stevioside at concentrations of 0, 2, 6, 10, 14, and 20% (w/v) to form gels. We systematically investigated how these sweeteners influenced the physical and rheological properties of the resulting fish gelatin gels—including color, gel strength, texture profile analysis (TPA), storage modulus (G′), loss modulus (G″), and viscosity. Results revealed that both sweeteners induced similar trends in color and viscosity changes across all tested concentrations. In contrast, their effects on TPA parameters and viscoelastic properties (G′ and G″) differed markedly—likely attributable to structural differences between xylitol and stevioside. Specifically, xylitol’s linear molecular structure facilitates multiple intermolecular interactions with fish gelatin, including ionic interactions, hydrogen bonding, van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic associations. These favorable interactions, combined with xylitol’s higher solubility and greater number of hydroxyl (–OH) groups, position it as a particularly promising sugar substitute for fish gelatin-based gels.

“Alright, then—what *is* this?” KX88 asked.  

I rubbed the bridge of my nose. “Before you react strongly again—this is normal. Completely normal.”  

“I didn’t ask whether it was normal!” He clutched his head. “Oh—*shit*. My brain feels hot and itchy. What’s happening? It’s *hot and itchy*!”  

I placed my hands firmly on his shoulders to steady him and prevent another outburst of flailing. “You’re experiencing anger. We call this *anger*. Your brain isn’t literally hot—it’s just how the sensation manifests for you right now.”  

“This is what anger *feels* like? That’s absurd! God, this used to be so much simpler—back when emotional states just registered as minor drops in processing efficiency.”  

Sitting him down had been the right call. I guided him gently toward a chair. “So that’s how you used to recognize anger?”  

“Yeah,” he said, pausing. “Well—other indicators, too. Like floating-point operation latency increasing…”  

“Now you have to *feel* it instead.”  

He picked up a glass of water from the table. “How do I scratch it?”  

“What?”  

“My brain. It’s hot and itchy. How do I *scratch it*?”  

I glanced upward, exhaling slowly. “You don’t. You manage the emotion—not the sensation. Anger will subside when the feeling passes.”  

He slammed the glass onto the table. “The cause hasn’t changed! Can’t you just compensate for it?”  

“Not really. Physical movement sometimes helps—like going for a walk. Or shifting focus: thinking about something pleasant. I even watch cartoons occasionally.”  

He growled in frustration. “Fuck—listen to that. The fan’s making noise again.”  

I pivoted smoothly. “To answer your original question—that mark on your skin came from where you were leaning against the edge of the table. It caused temporary erythema—the red line is where the pressure indented your skin. It’ll resolve on its own.”  

“Resolve? *Pop back out?* That’s disgusting.”  

A quiet, wry laugh escaped me. “That’s honestly the *least* disturbing thing the human body does on a daily basis.”  

His voice dropped, strained and raw. “I want to go back into the machine. This is… unbearable. I can *feel everything*—constantly reminded that clothes are touching me, that the AC airflow is brushing my skin like an intrusion. It’s all just unrelenting sensory noise—and I can’t regulate any of it. It’s overwhelming.” A sob broke through.  

I recognized the trajectory immediately. Without a word, I stood—quietly, swiftly—and moved to retrieve a box of tissues before things escalated further.  

Then—suddenly—he screamed: “*Fuck!* My eyes—they’ve *broken*! I’m leaking brain fluid!”  

Jesus Christ.

Nobody’s worth it

title: Effect and Molecular Mechanisms of Traditional Chinese Medicine on Tumor Targeting Tumor-Associated Macrophages
human: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has been used as a significant cancer treatment method for many years in China. It has been demonstrated that TCM could assist in inhibiting the growth of tumors and prolonging the survival rates of cancer patients. Although the mechanism of TCM are still not clear, accumulating evidence has shown that they may be related to the tumor microenvironment (TME). Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) play a significant role in TME and are polarized to two phenotypes, M1 (classically activated) and M2 (alternatively activated) TAMs. The two different phenotypes of TAMs play converse roles in the TME and M2-polarized tumor-associated macrophages (M2-TAMs) always lead to poor prognosis in cancer patients compared to M1-polarized tumor-associated macrophages (M1-TAMs). In this review, the potential correlation between TCM and TAMs (especially the M2 phenotype) in tumor progression and promising TCM strategies targeting TAMs in cancer are discussed.

title: Pullulan dialdehyde crosslinked gelatin hydrogels with high strength for biomedical applications
human: Herein the construction of a strong gelatin hydrogel is presented by using pullulan dialdehyde (PDA) as a macromolecular crosslinker. The resultant PDA crosslinked gelatin hydrogels (G-PDA) exhibit extremely high mechanical strength, manifested in the achieved optimal compressive stress of 5.80 MPa at 80% strain, which is up to 152 times higher than pure gelatin hydrogel. The G-PDA were characterized by Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The extent of crosslinking was determined by ninhydrin assay. The results suggested that the synergistic effect of dual-crosslinking, which is composed of short- and long-range covalent crosslinking and thermoreversible physical crosslinking, may played a key role in enhancing the load-bearing capacity of ensuing hydrogels. The swelling and enzymatic degradation of G-PDA are gradually limited with increasing PDA concentration. The result from MTT assay demonstrated that G-PDA is non-cytotoxic against MC3T3 cells, regardless of the concentrations of PDA.
text: Here, we present a robust gelatin hydrogel fabricated using pullulan dialdehyde (PDA) as a macromolecular crosslinker. The resulting PDA-crosslinked gelatin hydrogels (G-PDA) exhibit exceptional mechanical strength, achieving an optimal compressive stress of 5.80 MPa at 80% strain—up to 152 times greater than that of pure gelatin hydrogel. G-PDA hydrogels were characterized by Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), while the degree of crosslinking was quantified via ninhydrin assay. Results suggest that the enhanced load-bearing capacity arises from a synergistic dual-crosslinking mechanism—comprising both covalent (short- and long-range) and thermoreversible physical crosslinks. Swelling and enzymatic degradation of G-PDA decrease progressively with increasing PDA concentration. MTT assays confirmed that G-PDA is non-cytotoxic to MC3T3 cells across all tested PDA concentrations.

The Eighteenth Century America Report (Assessment)

Table of Contents
 1. Introduction
 2. Social changes
 3. Economic changes
 4. Cultural changes
 5. Political changes
 6. Conclusion
 7. Works Cited

Introduction

The rise of the British Empire began after successful explorations by Spain and Portugal. The King of England commissioned John Cabot to undertake explorations and conquer undiscovered lands. He came upon the Americas but he believed he had found Asia. This was the beginning of numerous explorations by England.

The British Empire began by taking up settlements and setting up plantations in America. They later moved to Africa where they colonized a majority of the land there. With the acquisition of the colonies in the Americas and Africa the British in the 1700s began developments in these colonies. These developments had social, political, economic and cultural impacts (Nicholas Canny 55).

Social changes

There were a number of social changes observed in the British colonies. There was an increase in the population in the colonies because of the increase in settlement of the colonizers. In the colonies the resources and all decisions were controlled by the wealthy. This made them the centre of the society.

There was the rise of different type of religions within the colonies. The rise of Christianity in most colonies would give people a sense of belonging. There was a rise in slavery and slave trade in the colonies. The slaves were shipped from Africa and brought to the Americas to work on the plantations, mines and as servants (Burk &Kathleen 67).

Economic changes

There was an increase in economic activities being done in the colonies. There was establishment of plantations, mines and industries to process goods. The British developed systems where they would get raw materials from the colonies and ship them back to be used in their factories in England. They got cheap and free labor from the slaves thus increasing the wealth of the rich settlers.

The growth of the triangular trade led to establishment of companies that traded in slaves and other goods produced in the colonies. This led to development of an extremely rich class that controlled activates in the colonies. There was also taxation that was developed in the colonies so that England would make money from the trade (Burk &Kathleen 78).

Cultural changes

There was a huge change in the cultures in the colonies. Many of the settlers brought new cultures into the colonies. They forced the indigenous people of the colonies to adopt these cultures. This saw the original inhabitants begin practicing the white man’s culture.

The increase in slave trade also saw a shift in the number of black people in the Americas. The slaves developed a culture that combined their various cultures. It was a fusion of their culture, that of the indigenous inhabitants and that of the settlers. Religions also influenced the cultures that were created by the people in the colonies (Nicholas Canny 98).

Political changes

The British brought their own political structures to the colonies. In spite f the fact that the colonies had certain social and leadership structures in place the British replaced them with their own systems that were believed to be more effective. The main people who were tasked with governing the colonies and developing laws are the rich people. These were the lords of the trade and the plantations. These were the wealthy people who controlled many aspects in the colony (Burk &Kathleen 122).

Conclusion

The colonies benefited and experienced negative changes from the colonialists. In America the changes were cut short before the 1800s when the colony became independent.
