title: An Examination of Factors Associated With Student Resiliency
human: Student resiliency, success, and retention are top priorities for nursing programs. The purpose of the cross-sectional descriptive study was to identify factors associated with the resiliency level and physical and mental health of nursing students. A cross-sectional descriptive study design was used with a convenience sample of 199 nursing students from organizations that comprise the Community Patient Safety Coalition Nursing Research Consortium. Resiliency was measured with the Connor Davidson Resiliency Scale. Physical and mental health was measured with the Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Global Health Short Form. Most of the nursing students in the sample were female (92%), White (94%), and in BSN programs (74.4%). Students had low resiliency (P < .0001) and low physical and mental health (P < .0001) compared with the general population. Student resilience was positively correlated to self-perception of physical and mental health.
text: Student resilience, success, and retention are top priorities for nursing programs. This cross-sectional descriptive study aimed to identify factors associated with resilience levels as well as physical and mental health among nursing students. A convenience sample of 199 nursing students—drawn from organizations within the Community Patient Safety Coalition Nursing Research Consortium—participated. Resilience was assessed using the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale, and physical and mental health were measured using the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS®) Global Health Short Form. The majority of participants were female (92%), White (94%), and enrolled in BSN programs (74.4%). Compared with the general U.S. population, students reported significantly lower resilience (p < .0001) and significantly poorer physical and mental health (p < .0001). Notably, higher resilience was positively correlated with more favorable self-perceptions of physical and mental health.

title: Koi herpesvirus (KHV) and KHV disease (KHVD) - a recently updated overview
human: Over the last years, there has been an enormous increase in the knowledge on koi herpesvirus (KHV), koi herpesvirus disease (KHVD), pathogenesis and virus variants. Different KHV lineages have clearly been identified, possible genomic changes during replication in different cell cultures at different temperatures but also in several hosts have been identified, a persistent stage of infection has been specified and it has been shown that infection with KHV is not host specific at all, but KHVD is. Additionally, it has been shown that it is possible to combat KHVD by immunization with inactivated and attenuated live vaccines using different delivery systems but also to benefit from alternative treatments with e.g. exopolysaccharids obtained from Arthrospira platensis.
text: In recent years, significant advances have been made in understanding koi herpesvirus (KHV), koi herpesvirus disease (KHVD), viral pathogenesis, and genetic diversity. Distinct KHV lineages have been clearly characterized, and genomic variations—arising during replication in diverse cell cultures, across varying temperatures, and in multiple host species—have been documented. A persistent phase of infection has been defined, and while KHV itself exhibits broad host susceptibility, clinical KHVD remains host-specific. Furthermore, effective control strategies have been developed, including immunization with both inactivated and attenuated live vaccines delivered via multiple routes. Complementary approaches, such as treatment with exopolysaccharides derived from *Arthrospira platensis*, have also demonstrated therapeutic potential.

title: Rare earth and financial markets: Dynamics of return and volatility connectedness around the COVID-19 outbreak
human: This study examines the return and volatility connectedness between the rare earth stock market and clean energy markets, world equity, base metals, gold, and crude oil. Using daily data from September 21, 2010 to August 28, 2020, a time-varying parameter vector autoregression (TVP-VAR) approach to connectedness is applied to uncover the dynamics of connectedness during the entire period and the COVID-19 pandemic period. Volatility connectedness is generally stronger than return connectedness. However, the return and volatility connectedness pattern varies over the full sample period, exhibiting a significant spike following the abrupt COVID-19 outbreak in February-March 2020. The rare earth index shows a close interdependence with the clean energy, world equity, and oil indexes during the outbreak of the pandemic, though it mostly remains a return and volatility receiver over the entire period. During the COVID-19 outbreak, the rare earth stock index becomes more central to the network of connectedness for both return and volatility, showing strong interdependence with clean energy and world equity. The volatility of the rare earth stock index exhibits a strong interdependence with that of crude oil prices. Our findings help investors understand diversification benefits and investment protection. They support policymakers in developing strategies for lessening import dependence on rare earth metals.
text:
This study investigates return and volatility connectedness between the rare earth stock market and several key asset classes: clean energy equities, global equity indices, base metals, gold, and crude oil. Employing daily data spanning September 21, 2010, to August 28, 2020, we apply a time-varying parameter vector autoregression (TVP-VAR) framework to trace the evolution of connectedness over the full sample period—and particularly during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.  

We find that volatility spillovers are consistently stronger than return spillovers. Nevertheless, both types of connectedness exhibit marked time variation, with a pronounced surge emerging in February–March 2020—immediately following the abrupt global outbreak of the pandemic. Throughout the full sample, the rare earth index predominantly acts as a net receiver of return and volatility spillovers. Yet during the pandemic’s initial phase, its role shifts significantly: it becomes more central within the broader connectedness network for both returns and volatility, displaying heightened interdependence with clean energy and global equity markets. Notably, the volatility of the rare earth index shows particularly strong linkages with crude oil price volatility.  

These findings offer practical insights for investors seeking optimal portfolio diversification and hedging strategies. They also provide timely evidence to inform policymakers aiming to reduce strategic import dependence on rare earth elements.

title: Students' achievement motivation in Finnish and Chinese higher education and its relation to perceived teaching-learning environments
human: This cross-cultural study of Finnish and Chinese students set out to compare the levels of achievement motivation (AM) in order to investigate whether the differences in them might be explained by the different cultural response styles and whether these response styles could be controlled for with a method which includes response style variables as covariates in ANCOVA. This study also scrutinizes relationships between perceived teaching-learning environments (TLE) and AM within each cultural group. The survey sample consisted of 3,035 Finnish and 2,309 mainland Chinese university students. Finnish students were found to rate the level of AM markedly higher than do Chinese students. It was determined that the method applied for response style controlling is not suitable for cross-cultural studies, even though it is recommended for this use. A modification of the method, which is based on robust statistical tools, was found not to change this conclusion, but it can nevertheless be used to obtain useful information about the effects of response style differences. The results also show that similar relationships between AM and TLE could be identified in the data of both groups. However, for the Finnish group AM is related to perceived suitable workload, whereas for the Chinese group it is related to teacher encouragement.
text: This cross-cultural study compared achievement motivation (AM) levels among 3,035 Finnish and 2,309 mainland Chinese university students. Its primary aim was to determine whether observed differences in AM could be attributed to culturally distinct response styles—and whether those styles could be statistically controlled using an ANCOVA approach that treats response style variables as covariates. A secondary aim was to examine how perceived teaching–learning environments (TLE) relate to AM within each cultural group. Results revealed that Finnish students reported significantly higher AM than their Chinese counterparts. However, the recommended ANCOVA method for controlling response styles proved unsuitable for cross-cultural comparisons—even after modification with robust statistical techniques. While this modified approach did not alter the core conclusion, it nonetheless yielded valuable insights into how response style differences influence AM estimates. Finally, similar overall patterns emerged between AM and TLE across both groups; yet the specific TLE dimensions linked to AM differed: workload appropriateness predicted AM among Finnish students, whereas teacher encouragement predicted AM among Chinese students.

text:
Most brightly colored birds inhabit tropical and subtropical regions, where abundant, intense sunlight prevails year-round. It is precisely this strong solar radiation that enhances and intensifies the vivid pigmentation in their plumage—colors as brilliant and varied as those of the rainbow.

Among these striking avian species, flamingos are especially notable—not only for their extraordinary appearance but also for their highly social behavior. Flamingos live in large, cohesive flocks. Historically, they were widespread across parts of the Americas; substantial populations once thrived in Florida, though today they are nearly extirpated from the United States. Their current strongholds lie primarily in Africa and southern Asia, with smaller, scattered populations also found in parts of Europe.

Flamingos select secluded wetland habitats—typically lakes or slow-moving rivers within dense jungle or marshland—to establish their colonies. There, they construct simple yet distinctive nests: mounds of mud elevated slightly above ground level, each featuring a shallow depression at the summit where the female lays her eggs. In favorable conditions, tens of thousands of individuals may congregate in a single location—such a dense aggregation is termed a *flamingo colony*.

Physically, the flamingo is an exceptionally tall wading bird—often exceeding human height when standing upright. Its long, slender legs and elongated neck are key adaptations for foraging: it stands motionless in shallow water, legs submerged like stilts, then bends its sinuous neck to submerge its uniquely shaped beak and filter-feed on small aquatic organisms—including algae, crustaceans, and tiny fish. Remarkably, prey often fails to flee upon seeing the flamingo’s legs, mistaking them for emergent reeds or stems.

When viewed en masse from a distance—whether gathered around a lake or aligned along a riverbank—the sight is truly majestic. Their plumage displays a vibrant, rosy-red hue, often edged with soft pink or white, lending the entire flock the appearance of a vast, living regiment clad in crimson uniforms.

This visual illusion has historical resonance: in earlier centuries, European travelers crossing African landscapes occasionally reported spotting what appeared to be disciplined troops in red coats assembled beside remote lakes—only to discover, upon closer inspection, that they were observing flamingos. Yet approaching such colonies was—and remains—exceptionally difficult. Like certain wild ungulates, flamingos employ dedicated *sentinels*: vigilant individuals stationed at the periphery of the feeding area who maintain constant watch and issue loud alarm calls at the first sign of danger.

Equally breathtaking is the spectacle of a flamingo flock in flight. Soaring high above the landscape in perfect formation, they resemble a luminous, airborne cloud bathed in the radiant hues of sunset—blending deep rose, coral, and tangerine. Thousands fly in precise, disciplined rows and ranks, maintaining uniform altitude and spacing—a natural aerial phalanx.

Another brilliantly colored, gregarious jungle bird is the parrot. While many are familiar with captive parrots—often seen in cages or tethered to perches—their wild counterparts lead vastly different lives. Native to warm, sun-drenched regions across the globe, parrots thrive in dense, biodiverse forests and travel in lively, vocal flocks.

Wild parrots also nest colonially. A compelling example is found in India, at the abandoned city of Amber. Once the opulent capital of a powerful Rajput kingdom, Amber was home to a magnificent marble palace built by its ruler, alongside grand residences for nobles and courtiers—all crafted from gleaming white marble. At the monarch’s command, however, the entire population relocated to found a new capital, leaving Amber intact and uninhabited. Today, the city stands remarkably preserved: pristine marble palaces and mansions rise serenely against the azure sky, encircled by flourishing thickets of wild red roses.

Imagine the scene: the vivid blue expanse overhead, carpets of crimson roses below, and luminous white architecture in between—animated by countless emerald-green parrots darting across the sky and flitting effortlessly from palace balcony to rose-laden bough. The landscape becomes a living tapestry woven from bold bands of red, white, and blue.

title: In Silico Prediction of Metabolic Epoxidation for Drug-like Molecules via Machine Learning Methods
human: Epoxidation is one of the reactions in drug metabolism. Since epoxide metabolites would bind with proteins or DNA covalently, drugs should avoid epoxidation metabolism in the body. Due to the instability of epoxide, it is difficult to determine epoxidation experimentally. In silico models based on big data and machine learning methods are hence valuable approaches to predict whether a compound would undergo epoxidation. In this study, we collected 884 epoxidation data manually from various sources, and finally got 829 unique sites of epoxidation. Three types of molecular fingerprints with different lengths (1024, 2048 or 4096 bits) were used to describe the reaction sites. Six machine learning methods were used to build the classification models. The training set and test set were randomly divided into 8 : 2, and 54 models were constructed and evaluated. Four best models were selected for feature selection. The features were then chosen and verified by external validation set. The resulted optimal model had the accuracy and AUC (area under the curve) values at 0.873 and 0.944 for the test set, 0.838 and 0.987 for the external validation set, respectively. The models built in this study could accurately predict whether a compound will undergo epoxidation and which part is most susceptible to epoxidation, which is of great significance for drug design.
text:
Epoxidation is a key metabolic pathway in drug metabolism. Because epoxide metabolites can covalently bind to proteins and DNA—potentially leading to toxicity—minimizing or avoiding epoxidation is a critical objective in drug design. However, the inherent chemical instability of epoxides makes their experimental detection and characterization challenging. Consequently, in silico prediction models—leveraging large-scale data and machine learning—are highly valuable for identifying compounds prone to epoxidation.  

In this study, we manually curated 884 experimentally reported epoxidation events from diverse literature and databases, yielding 829 unique, chemically validated epoxidation sites. To encode structural features around each reaction site, we employed three types of molecular fingerprints—1024-, 2048-, and 4096-bit ECFP4 fingerprints. Six distinct machine learning algorithms were used to build binary classification models predicting epoxidation susceptibility at specific sites. The dataset was randomly partitioned into training and test sets at an 8:2 ratio, resulting in 54 model variants (3 fingerprint types × 6 algorithms × 3 random splits), all rigorously evaluated. From these, the four top-performing models underwent systematic feature selection, followed by validation using an independent external dataset. The final optimized model achieved an accuracy of 0.873 and an AUC of 0.944 on the internal test set, and 0.838 and 0.987, respectively, on the external validation set. Collectively, these models enable accurate, site-specific prediction of epoxidation liability—providing a powerful tool to guide safer, more rational drug design.

title: Use of evidential reasoning and AHP to assess regional industrial safety
human: China's fast economic growth contributes to the rapid development of its urbanization process, and also renders a series of industrial accidents, which often cause loss of life, damage to property and environment, thus requiring the associated risk analysis and safety control measures to be implemented in advance. However, incompleteness of historical failure data before the occurrence of accidents makes it difficult to use traditional risk analysis approaches such as probabilistic risk analysis in many cases. This paper aims to develop a new methodology capable of assessing regional industrial safety (RIS) in an uncertain environment. A hierarchical structure for modelling the risks influencing RIS is first constructed. The hybrid of evidential reasoning (ER) and Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) is then used to assess the risks in a complementary way, in which AHP is hired to evaluate the weight of each risk factor and ER is employed to synthesise the safety evaluations of the investigated region(s) against the risk factors from the bottom to the top level in the hierarchy. The successful application of the hybrid approach in a real case analysis of RIS in several major districts of Beijing (capital of China) demonstrates its feasibility as well as provides risk analysts and safety engineers with useful insights on effective solutions to comprehensive risk assessment of RIS in metropolitan cities. The contribution of this paper is made by the findings on the comparison of risk levels of RIS at different regions against various risk factors so that best practices from the good performer(s) can be used to improve the safety of the others.

title: A machine learning framework to determine geolocations from metagenomic profiling
human: Studies on metagenomic data of environmental microbial samples found that microbial communities seem to be geolocation-specific, and the microbiome abundance profile can be a differentiating feature to identify samples' geolocations. In this paper, we present a machine learning framework to determine the geolocations from metagenomics profiling of microbial samples. Our method was applied to the multi-source microbiome data from MetaSUB (The Metagenomics and Metadesign of Subways and Urban Biomes) International Consortium for the CAMDA 2019 Metagenomic Forensics Challenge (the Challenge). The goal of the Challenge is to predict the geographical origins of mystery samples by constructing microbiome fingerprints.First, we extracted features from metagenomic abundance profiles. We then randomly split the training data into training and validation sets and trained the prediction models on the training set. Prediction performance was evaluated on the validation set. By using logistic regression with L2 normalization, the prediction accuracy of the model reaches 86%, averaged over 100 random splits of training and validation datasets.The testing data consists of samples from cities that do not occur in the training data. To predict the "mystery" cities that are not sampled before for the testing data, we first defined biological coordinates for sampled cities based on the similarity of microbial samples from them. Then we performed affine transform on the map such that the distance between cities measures their biological difference rather than geographical distance. After that, we derived the probabilities of a given testing sample from unsampled cities based on its predicted probabilities on sampled cities using Kriging interpolation. Results show that this method can successfully assign high probabilities to the true cities-of-origin of testing samples. Our framework shows good performance in predicting the geographic origin of metagenomic samples for cities where training data are available. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of the proposed method to predict metagenomic samples' geolocations for samples from locations that are not in the training dataset.
text:
Metagenomic analyses of environmental microbial samples have revealed that microbial communities exhibit strong geographic specificity, with microbiome abundance profiles serving as distinctive biomarkers for inferring sample origin. In this work, we introduce a machine learning framework designed to predict the geolocation of microbial samples directly from their metagenomic profiles. We applied this framework to multi-source microbiome data contributed by the MetaSUB (Metagenomics and Metadesign of Subways and Urban Biomes) International Consortium as part of the CAMDA 2019 Metagenomic Forensics Challenge—whose objective was to reconstruct the geographical origins of “mystery” samples using microbiome-based fingerprints.

Our approach begins with feature extraction from metagenomic abundance profiles. We then randomly partitioned the labeled training data into separate training and validation subsets, iteratively training predictive models on the former and evaluating performance on the latter. Using logistic regression with L2 regularization, our model achieved an average prediction accuracy of 86% across 100 independent random train–validation splits.

Critically, the test set comprised samples from cities entirely absent from the training data—posing a zero-shot geolocation inference problem. To address this, we first established *biological coordinates* for each city represented in the training set, derived from pairwise microbial profile similarities. We then applied an affine transformation to project these cities onto a biologically informed map, where inter-city distances reflect microbial dissimilarity rather than physical geography. Finally, for each unseen test city, we estimated its probability of origin using Kriging interpolation—leveraging the model’s predicted class probabilities over the biologically embedded training cities. Evaluation confirmed that the method consistently assigns high posterior probability to the true city-of-origin for test samples.

Collectively, our framework demonstrates robust performance in predicting geographic origins for cities represented in the training data, while also showing strong promise for generalizing to novel, previously unsampled locations—a key advance for metagenomic forensics and spatial microbiome epidemiology.

text:
Hello—I don’t know who you are, and you don’t know me. Not yet.  

I’ve stood exactly where you stand now: confused, terrified, and utterly hopeless. But keep reading. I’m about to tell you how to get out.  

My name is Rose—though that no longer matters. Like you, I woke up in this Godforsaken place with no memory of how or why I’d arrived. Let me be clear: this is not your fault. It’s part of something larger—something purposeful.  

This place exists beyond the norms and rules of the world outside. With every thunderous bang on the door, every plate of rotting food he forces upon you, and every roar of rain outside—rain that pounds against inches-thick concrete, stealing life one drop at a time—your mind will fray. What people told you beyond these walls holds no weight here. A diagnosis of “clinical insanity” from a doctor out there means nothing the moment you cross this threshold. Here, clinical insanity isn’t pathology—it’s survival. It’s the only sane response to an insane reality.  

You’re scanning these pages for answers, aren’t you? For a way out? I may not know your name—but I know you more deeply than you know yourself. You’re lying on this cold, unyielding floor, just as you have been for the past week. Every time the door opens and he stands there—naked—you weep for hours. Every time he speaks, you feel only hatred. Every time you see him, you want to tear your eyes from your skull. Does that sound familiar? Then congratulations: by the standards of the world outside, you’re as clinically insane as I am.  

You’re searching for salvation—a way out of this makeshift hell, built solely for the pleasure of the man I call my worst nightmare, and whom the world outside likely knows as a respected physician—or perhaps a celebrated author. There are always two sides to every story. Two sides to every coin: one polished and public, the other buried deep beneath the surface. But that duality means nothing to me anymore—because as I write these words, I am freer than I’ve ever been.  

So if you’re looking for a way out—know this: there is none.  
But if you’re seeking freedom? Stop thinking. Let yourself die inside.  
That is the only way you’ll ever truly live again.
